extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing USPTO guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo patent-eligibility test: identify additional claim elements beyond any judicial exception and determine whether those elements, individually and in combination, amount to an "inventive concept" (i.e., significantly more than the exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B inventive concept inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should answer by first identifying any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), then evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)). This evaluation is made with respect to the Supreme Court considerations introduced in MPEP § 2106 (and discussed in detail in subsections (a) through (h)). The evaluation is not a weighing test; it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to applicant's invention and whether the additional elements encompass an inventive concept. If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more than the exception (Step 2B: NO) it is not eligible; if it does (Step 2B: YES) it is eligible (Pathway C) and the eligibility analysis is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must identify whether there are any elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate those elements both individually and as an ordered combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether each additional element by itself is well-understood, routine, conventional activity or a generic implementation, and whether a combination of elements produces a non-conventional, non-generic arrangement that amounts to significantly more. Courts have emphasized that the inventive concept inquiry requires more than recognizing that each claim element, by itself, was known in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the specification and use broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of what the applicant has invented should be made by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with a reasonable interpretation (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the specification to determine how elements are described (e.g., whether elements are described as well-known generic components or as providing technical details/solutions). Use MPEP § 2111 for claim construction. The specification can show whether a technical problem and an unconventional technical solution are disclosed (examples: McRO vs Affinity Labs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology (improvement consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology or technical field (i.e., a technological solution to a technological problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration may be evaluated at Step 2A or Step 2B. The claim focus must be examined under BRI to determine whether the invention purports to improve technology. The specification should provide a technical explanation showing how to implement the invention so a person of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The claim itself must reflect the improvement (not merely the specification). Avoid oversimplifying claims; evaluate the claim as an ordered combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-functionality improvement criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities or instead merely uses computers as a tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that improves how a computer stores, retrieves, or processes data, or provides a specific implementation in software/architecture, may show an improvement (see Enfish, BASCOM, DDR, Amdocs, Visual Memory examples). Method claims must be limited to computer implementation to qualify; if the entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology. Courts have listed examples of improvements (e.g., modified Internet hyperlink protocol, inventive distribution of functionality in a network, specialized memory systems, specific GUIs, particular server structures) and examples that are insufficient (e.g., mere automation, using a general-purpose computer, mere speedups due to generic hardware).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to other technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims showing improvements in non-computer technologies or broader technical fields may demonstrate eligibility when they describe particular ways to solve technical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found eligibility where claims recite specific methods, devices, or configurations that improve a technological process (examples: Diamond v. Diehr thermocouple modification to rubber molding, particular telephone/server combinations, improved downloading for streaming, improved data compression, measurement devices generating new data, inertial sensor configurations, improved preservation processes). Claims must recite details on how a computer or other technology aids the method; merely adding generic components is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration (machine-or-transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the judicial exception is applied with, or by use of, a particular machine — the machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test is a useful clue for determining whether a claim is patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The M-or-T test is not a stand-alone test. All claims must still be evaluated under Alice/Mayo. If a claim passes Alice/Mayo it is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test; if it fails Alice/Mayo it is ineligible even if it passes M-or-T. When a machine is alleged, evaluate whether the machine elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception rather than being mere generic or conventional components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of machine/apparatus elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree to which the machine or apparatus in the claim can be specifically identified (not any and all machines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular machines with specific structural details (e.g., particular antenna shape/arrangement, Fourdrinier machine elements) can support eligibility; a general-purpose computer that applies an exception using conventional computer functions does not qualify as a particular machine. Adding generic computer components or a 'specially programmed' generic computer does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine implements the method steps (integral use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the machine plays an integral role in achieving the claimed method steps rather than merely serving as an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral use of a machine to achieve performance of a method may provide significantly more; if the machine merely serves as a medium or obvious mechanism to permit a solution to be achieved more quickly, it generally will not. (See CyberSource and Versata examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-solution activity and field-of-use limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation that imposes no meaningful limits on the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method (e.g., mere data-gathering from a source, or restricting use to a field of use) will not provide significantly more. Courts have held that data-gathering steps and nominal Internet sourcing do not make a claim statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation (transformation of an article)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing — a classic clue to patentability of a process claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of an article to a different state or thing is a relevant clue but not a stand-alone test. If such a transformation exists, the claim is likely to be significantly more than a judicial exception. Nonetheless, all claims must be evaluated under Alice/Mayo and the M-or-T clue must be weighed in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim analysis; dependent claims may differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine each claim for eligibility separately based on the particular elements recited therein; do not treat all claims in an application as automatically standing or falling together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One claim may be ineligible while a dependent claim that adds additional elements that amount to significantly more may be eligible. If a claim clearly recites multiple discrete exceptions, an examiner may select one exception to analyze for examination efficiency, but if the selected-exception analysis finds significantly more, treat the claim as eligible.
